posts.text: An owl can turn its head up to 270 degrees, and the reason has nothing to do with the neck. It starts with the eyes, and they are not built the way yours are. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: Owls Turn Their Heads 270 Degrees
alt: Photo of a owl above a cream band reading Owls Turn Their Heads 270 Degrees.

posts.text: Reindeer eyes are gold in summer and a deep blue by winter. They are the only mammals known to do it, and the switch has a job. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: Eyes That Turn Blue In Winter
alt: Photo of a reindeer above a cream band reading Eyes That Turn Blue In Winter.

posts.text: A diving peregrine falcon passes 240 mph, the fastest any animal moves. At that speed the air alone should wreck its lungs. Something in its nose stops that. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: Two Hundred Forty Miles An Hour
alt: Photo of a peregrine falcon above a cream band reading Two Hundred Forty Miles An Hour.

posts.text: A giant squid's eye runs up to 27 cm across, the largest in the animal kingdom, built for the faintest flicker of light in the deep.
posts.title: Eyes The Size Of Dinner Plates
alt: Photo of a giant squid above a cream band reading Eyes The Size Of Dinner Plates.

posts.text: Many bats fire up to 200 calls a second while flying in total darkness. Every one of those calls is doing a job. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: Two Hundred Calls A Second
alt: Photo of a bat above a cream band reading Two Hundred Calls A Second.

posts.text: Flamingos can stand, and even sleep, on one leg for hours, at almost no effort. There is a good reason they bother. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: The One-Leg Trick
alt: Photo of a flamingo above a cream band reading The One-Leg Trick.

posts.text: A giraffe's neck holds exactly seven vertebrae, the same number as a human neck. The famous 25 pound giraffe heart turns out to be a myth too.
posts.title: Seven Neck Bones, Same As You
alt: Photo of a giraffe above a cream band reading Seven Neck Bones, Same As You.

posts.text: Sea otters carry up to a million hairs per square inch, the densest fur of any animal. For an otter that is not a luxury, it is survival. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: A Million Hairs Per Inch
alt: Photo of a sea otter above a cream band reading A Million Hairs Per Inch.

posts.text: For decades everyone had the same explanation for how a Komodo dragon kills its prey. Then researchers actually looked, and it was wrong. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: The Komodo Dragon Story Was Wrong
alt: Photo of a komodo dragon above a cream band reading The Komodo Dragon Story Was Wrong.

posts.text: Platypus mothers make milk but have no nipples at all. The babies still get fed, just not the way any other mammal does it. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: Milk Without Nipples
alt: Photo of a platypus above a cream band reading Milk Without Nipples.

posts.text: Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards, and they can hover upside down for a moment. It comes down to one joint no other bird has. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: The Only Bird That Flies Backwards
alt: Photo of a hummingbird above a cream band reading The Only Bird That Flies Backwards.

posts.text: The quokka gets called the happiest animal in the world for that permanent grin. The grin is real. What causes it is not what it looks like. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: It Is Not Actually Smiling
alt: Photo of a quokka above a cream band reading It Is Not Actually Smiling.

posts.text: A shoebill can stand completely still over the water for hours. What happens when it finally moves is the whole point. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: The Statue That Hunts
alt: Photo of a shoebill above a cream band reading The Statue That Hunts.

posts.text: Meerkat mobs post a sentinel on a raised mound and swap the job about every hour so everyone gets to forage.
posts.title: The Lookout Shift Rotates
alt: Photo of a meerkat above a cream band reading The Lookout Shift Rotates.

posts.text: The aye-aye finds grubs hidden inside solid wood without ever seeing them. That strange middle finger is only half of how it does it. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: The Finger That Finds Grubs
alt: Photo of a aye-aye above a cream band reading The Finger That Finds Grubs.

posts.text: A toco toucan's bill makes up more than a third of its body surface. On a hot day, that bill is doing a very specific job. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: What A Toucan's Bill Is For
alt: Photo of a toco toucan above a cream band reading What A Toucan's Bill Is For.

posts.text: Giant manta rays have the largest brain for their body size of any fish. What they do in front of a mirror is the interesting part. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: The Ocean's Biggest Brain
alt: Photo of a giant manta ray above a cream band reading The Ocean's Biggest Brain.

posts.text: A fennec fox's ears reach 15 cm on an animal under two kilograms. Its hearing is excellent, but that is not mainly what the ears are for. The reason why → BeastlyFacts.com
posts.title: What Fennec Ears Are Really For
alt: Photo of a fennec fox above a cream band reading What Fennec Ears Are Really For.

posts.text: A cassowary's inner toe carries a claw over 4 inches long. Despite the reputation they are shy fruit eaters that would rather leave.
posts.title: The Dagger Toe
alt: Photo of a cassowary above a cream band reading The Dagger Toe.

posts.text: The kakapo is the only flightless parrot alive and the heaviest, nocturnal, and males boom a call that carries for miles.
posts.title: A Parrot That Forgot To Fly
